text: You could lose your savings to 7 scams, but only one of them almost nobody spots. I ran it. Which?
I'm Lenny. Ex-scammer. These days I take my old tricks apart, so they stop working on you.
Seven scams. The exact messages. And the one tell that gives each one away. Number seven is last, and it costs the most.
Number one. The delivery text.
Your parcel could not be delivered. Update your address here.
Here's the trick. You send it to thousands of people at once. Somebody is always waiting for a parcel.
They tap the link, and the page looks exactly like the courier. Logo, colours, tracking number.
It asks for a tiny redelivery fee. A couple of dollars. Nobody thinks twice.
But I never wanted the two dollars. I wanted the card number you just typed in.
The tell is the link. Real couriers don't send you to a random domain with extra words and numbers in it.
Waiting for a parcel? Open the courier's app yourself. Never the link.
Number two. The bank call. This one was my favourite.
Your phone shows your bank's name. A calm voice says there's a suspicious payment, and they need to verify you.
They know your name. Sometimes the last digits of your card. Feels real, right?
Caller ID can be faked. The name on your screen proves nothing. And those details? Old data leaks. Not your bank.
Then comes the ask. Read me the code we just texted you. That code is the key to your account.
So say this. I'll call you back on the number on my card. A real bank says fine. I used to hang up.
That's two down. Number three gets grandparents every single day. And number seven? Stay with me.
Number three. Hi Mum, I dropped my phone, this is my new number.
A few messages of small talk. Then an urgent bill that has to be paid today, from your account, not theirs.
And there's always a reason they can't just call. Broken phone. Broken microphone. In a meeting.
The tell is urgency, plus a new number, plus money. Call the old number. If your kid picks up, you're done.
And agree on a family code word now, before anyone needs it. I hated families with code words.
Number four. The easy job.
A friendly recruiter messages you out of nowhere. Money for liking videos or rating hotels. You never applied. That's the first tell.
The first payments are real. Small, but real. That's the bait.
Then a task needs you to top up your account to unlock bigger earnings. And then one more. And one more.
That's the switch. Any job that asks you to pay in is not a job.
Number five. The keen buyer.
You list something online. A buyer agrees instantly. No haggling, no questions about the item.
They send a link to receive your payment. The link asks for your card details, including the code on the back.
You never need that to receive money. Only to send it.
A real buyer has questions. A scammer has a link.
Number six. The frozen screen.
A pop-up fills the screen. Sirens. Your computer is infected, call this number now.
If you call, a helpful technician asks you to install a program, so he can fix it. That program gives him your computer. And your bank.
Real security software never gives you a phone number. Close the browser. Restart if you have to. Never call.
And number seven. The one almost nobody spots.
It doesn't start with a scam. It starts with a wrong number. Hi, is this Anna?
You say no. They're sorry. They're nice. A little funny. So you keep chatting. For weeks.
They're successful. They trade crypto or gold. They never push it. One day, you ask how it works.
You put in a little. The dashboard shows profit. You even withdraw a small amount. So you put in more.
Then you try to take it all out. There's a tax. A fee. Then another fee. The platform was never real.
And the person you talked to every day? A script. I know. I used to write them.
Why nobody spots it? There's no single moment that feels like a scam. Every step is small.
So here's the tell. Someone you've never met in person, bringing up money, is the whole scam. That kindness was the product.
Every one of these seven breaks the same rule. They want you to act inside their message. Their link. Their number. Their platform.
The defence is always the same. Leave the message. Slow down. Open your bank, your courier, your family's number yourself.
A real problem will still be there in ten minutes. A scam won't.
Already clicked, or already paid? Call your bank on the number on the back of your card. Right now. Speed matters.
Change your passwords. Turn on two-step verification. If someone installed software, disconnect and get it checked. Then report it.
And watch for recovery services that promise your money back for a fee. Same scam, round two.
And don't be embarrassed. These scams are built by people who do this all day. People like the old me.
If one of these would have got someone you know, send them this video. That's the whole job.
Trust me. I used to run all seven.
